AFRICRYPT CRYPTO HEIST

By: Latashia Naidoo | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We investigate how two brothers - barely out of their teens - managed to disappear with billions in investors' monies, in one of the world's largest crypto scams

Unique Selling Point:
An international manhunt is underway for two Durban brothers - Ameer and Raees Cajee, the founders of crypto investment firm, Africrypt, who are alleged to have fled the country with an estimated R54 billion worth of crypto assets - all from investors.

Thanks to digital forensic evidence and exclusive access to the brothers' bank statements, we go in search of the missing billions, and expose a life of decadence and excess - amassed through lies, fraudulent activities, and selling investors a 'dream'.

Summary:
How did two Durban brothers - barely out of their teens - manage to scarper as much as an alleged R51.27 billion worth of digital coins from investors off their little-known cryptocurrency platform?
That’s the question everyone’s been asking since AfriCrypt founders, Raees (21) and Ameer (18) Cajee, first announced a platform “breach” to their investors in April 2021.
They claimed that the company had been hacked, and all its cryptocurrency holdings stolen - to the tune of billions of rand.

Since then, the brothers have fled the country - purportedly for fear of their lives - all while a sordid tale of greed, excess and deception has been unfolding back home - in what some experts claim could be one of the biggest crypto scams in history.
Africrypt claimed to be a wildly successful cryptocurrency investment platform in which investors would send funds for the Cajee brothers to trade.

The platform surged in popularity in 2020 as word spread of the huge gains being made, but in 2021 a familiar pattern began to emerge – there were problems with withdrawals, then communications stalled, and finally the platform collapsed, taking investor funds with it.
While it’s now understood a group of about 15 investors who have been pressing for liquidation of AfriCrypt had invested about R100 million in the platform, the total amount invested could run into billions - with some putting the figure at $3.6 billion (R51.27 billion.)

If correct, this would far exceed the $588 million netted by Mirror Trading International, rated one of the biggest crypto scams of 2020.

And while the Financial Sector Conduct Authority’s (FSCA’s) is investigating Africrypt, a group of some 35 investors have now hired Durban-based PI, Sean Peirce, to track down the brothers, piece together the funds’ disappearance, and bring the pair to book.

Now investors say they won’t stop baying for blood, until justice is served.


Further information:
I have access to court records, bank statements, and investors who lost tens of millions with AfriCrypt and are willing to speak on record.

The investigators further claim that there are other criminal elements to this case - including money laundering.

Peirce adds that the Cajee’s “went wild with other people’s monies”, and has visual and social media documentation of the brother’s fleet of super cars, lavish dwellings, private jets, and eye-wateringly expensive family holidays - just months before the reported “hack”.

Press Release:


The Multi-Billion Rand Heist
They rose to stratospheric heights of wealth after starting Africa’s largest and most successful trading company, allegedly driven by artificial intelligence trading bots, from their tiny bedroom. Then they said a hack saw the company lose a staggering R54 billion practically overnight. Investors suffered crippling losses, with some individuals having invested millions of rands. But was this the hack of the century or an inside job? Carte Blanche unravels the true South African fairytale of the 18- and 21-year-old brothers who went from rags to multi-million rand riches as wealthy investors trusted the persuasive teenagers with their millions. Carte Blanche unravels how the two brothers ended up fleeing the country, while Interpol works on their extradition and liquidators try to track down missing funds.
Producer: Latashia Naidoo | Presenter: Masa Kekana


Script:


AFRICRYPT SCRIPT:

WIKIMEDIA PICS OF AMEER AND RAEES; PICS OF AFRICRYPT LOGO, PICS OF THE UMHLANGA AND THE BALLITO MAGAZINES
VO:
It was the quintessential rags to riches South African fairytale - of two child prodigies who started a cryptocurrency business out of a tiny bedroom in Robertsham, south of Johannesburg, back in 2013 - before growing it into one of Africa’s largest and most successful AI trading companies.
Or so they claimed.

PICS: HEADLINES

VO:
Fast forward to April 2021, when the fairytale turned into a financial nightmare for investors of the brothers’ cryptocurrency investment scheme, Africrypt.

VO:
On April 13, founders Ameer and Raees Cajee, announced a hack of their AI-driven trading platform – before fleeing the country – allegedly with billions worth of bitcoin from client wallets in tow, in what’s now been alleged to be an ‘exit scam’.
PIC: HEADLINE 1

VO:
Some estimates put the loss at a mind-blowing $3.6 billion – or R54 billion at the time of the incident.

LINK:
Main Camera Card 2 1308 - NINJAV_S002_S001_T072 – 00’31 – 01’02
It has all the makings of a major Hollywood blockbuster: two young men with a penchant for supercars, designer labels and private jets; an international manhunt, and billions in stolen cash. But in the real-life version of the Africrypt crypto heist saga, the criminal masterminds are in fact two brothers from Johannesburg – barely out of their teens – who’ve allegedly managed to swindle billions from investors, all while evading local and international authorities.


HEADLINE 15; AFRICRYPT BITCOIN SNAPSHOT, BITCOIN WALLET PICS

VO:
The Cajee brothers allegedly transferred 69,000 bitcoin during the so-called ‘hack’ – to various dark web tumblers and mixers - to make the funds untraceable.

FOOTAGE FROM YOUTUBE VIDEO OF LIFESTYLE (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vW9G9vVCopg&t=4s)
VO:

But who are the so-called “Crypto Brothers” at the helm of what some are calling one of the biggest crypto scams in history?

GRAPHIC: PIC – BROTHERS (INVESTOR PRESENTATION AND PICS IN FOLDER)
VO:
At 21, Raees Cajee is the CEO and founder of Africrypt. In an investor presentation from 2020, he claims to have started the company when he was just 13. And that he first learned of Bitcoin in 2009, and became an early adopter of the cryptocurrency.

VO:
Brother Ameer Cajee, 18, is the company’s COO – who claims he was a personal equity trader for two years - before branching out into derivative trading.
PIC: CAJEES 2
PIC: ABOUT PICS, 20 MONTH TRADING RESULT GRAPHIC SHOWING TIERS
VIZ: INVESTOR VIDEO

VO: Since Africrypt’s official launch in 2019, the Cajee brothers received millions of rands in deposits from investors who were promised seductive monthly profits of approximately 10% - offered through three tiers of investment packages: Passive, Passive Aggressive, and Aggressive.

PIC: AFRICRYPT IPHONE VIDEO (PLEASE ADD THE WORD ‘HACK’ ACROSS); INVESTOR EMAIL – HIGHLIGHT FIRST PARAGRAPH
VO:
Then came the bombshell announcement: the Africrypt platform had been hacked – allegedly by an unknown and malicious entity in the Ukraine. Ameer Cajee emailed investors on April 13 to tell them that all their bitcoin holdings had been stolen. The brothers fled to the UK shortly after.

PIC: INVESTOR EMAIL – HIGHLIGHT THIRD PARAGRAPH
DARREN: Second camera card, 13.08, 0001: 03’28 – 03’42
“The person conveying the message also told clients: ‘Do not contact lawyers, do not contact law enforcement, that would only slow down the recovery process.’ That to us was concerning.

VO:
Darren Hanekom of Hanekom Attorneys is representing a consortium of disgruntled former Africrypt investors. He suggests that a hack of the platform was highly implausible – given that the Cajee brothers were the only ones in control of the private keys to the blockchain network.

DARREN: SECOND CAMERA 13.08, 00’55 – 01’08
“If it was indeed a hack, and if it was a hack of the blockchain, it would be the first hack of the bitcoin network.”
MASA: MAIN CAMERA CARD 1 12.08, T004, 15’02 – 15’04: “How much money are we talking here?”

DARREN: Second camera card, 13.08, 0003: 02’08 – 03’06:
“When it comes to the exact amount in question, we’ve seen presentations of the Cajee’s website which alludes to $500m under management. We’ve also seen client totals up to R300m. But then, at the same time, we’ve also observed that the crypto addresses are within the billions. Right now, the only people who know exactly how much is involved, are the Cajee brothers.”

VO: For Durban businessman Luis Farais, the Africrypt alleged scam was the ultimate betrayal. Farais developed a close, personal friendship with the entire Cajee family – before their business relationship turned sour.
LUIS: Main camera card 1 12.08, T015: 02’27 – 02’57
“In total, over time, as the relationship built, and there was more trust and surety – and I also built that relationship to safeguard my investment… - and I built it up between me and my children to R7.5 million at the time they said to us the supposed hack had happened.”

VO:
As an established businessman, Farais knew the risks all too well – bitcoin could offer fast ascends on investments, and equally spectacular plunges. But he was convinced by the Cajee brothers of guaranteed returns – and prompted to keep investing more and more.

LUIS: Main camera card 1 12.08, T015: 10’46 – 11’15
“After meeting Raees mainly – and Ameer – but the one I dealt with most was Raees, his intelligence was just next level. Some have made him out to be a prodigy – I wouldn’t say that but he’s a very intelligent youngster. And he’s so knowledgeable in terms of the crypto market, in terms of laws around the world. And just so advanced.”

LINK: Main Camera Card 2 13.08 - NINJAV_S002_S001_T081 – 00’04 – 00’31
The investors we’ve spoken to all claimed that the Cajee brothers “walked the walk and talked the talk” when it came to crypto investments. They were also unapologetic about flaunting their extensive wealth, as is evident in this video - shot by the Cajee’s friends - which offers a glimpse into their audacious spending habits, and the lifestyle of two young brothers living large and playing hard.

PIC: PAGE 177/203 OF BADASPEX AFFIDAVIT (HIGHLIGHT SECOND AMOUNT ON 4 NOVEMBER, 12 NOVEMBER, BIG AMOUNT ON 26 NOVEMBER, 8 DECEMBER, LEATHER JACKETS ON 20 JANUARY)

VO:
The brother’s lavish spending habits are further illustrated in court papers. Expenses from the company account include: business class tickets to the Maldives for 5 people for R495 000; and R263000 for watches.

VIZ: (CAN WE GET A WORLD MAP GRAPHIC AND HIGHLIGHT THESE CITIES IN RED?)

VO: Since leaving South Africa in mid-April, the Cajees have been playing cat and mouse with investors and investigators alike - in places like Dubai, Doha, London, the Maldives, and Tanzania.

LINK: MAIN CAMERA CARD 12.08, T035, 00’04 – 00’28
The Cajee brothers led an ostentatious lifestyle, which included multi-million rand cars, business class travel to island paradises, and rentals in some of the country’s most upmarket establishments – including the Zimbali Coastal Estate in Ballito, north of Durban, where they allegedly paid R60 000 per month for a year-long rental in a multi-million rand luxury property.

GRAPHIC – WORLD MAP WITH VANUATU HIGHLIGHTED

VO:
In October 2020, Raees Cajee obtained citizenship in the Pacific Island nation of Vanuatu through the country’s citizenship-by-investment scheme, with his brother following suit in January 2021.

PIC: VANUATU PAMPHLET

VO:
Some experts have warned that the scheme is ripe for exploitation, creating a backdoor for visa-free access to the EU and UK.

SEAN: MAIN CAMERA CARD 2, 13.08, TO57: 05:44 – 05’54 – “It’s pretty obvious. Why would you get citizenship in another country without extradition orders, if you weren’t planning an exit strategy – or a so-called hack?”

VO:
Sean Peirce is a specialist investigator who has been mandated by 35 investors to track down the Cajee brothers.

SEAN: MAIN CAMERA CARD 2, 13.08, TO57: 02’07 -
“These guys are pretty clever with software and algorithms, but they’re not very clever with the law and how bank accounts work, and how we follow the money. And we’ve been following the money!”

MASA: 0’06’21 – 0’06’24: “How confident are you that you will be able to cuff them?”

SEAN: MAIN CAMERA CARD 2, 13.08, TO57: 08’05 – 08’21: “These kids – and they’re kids – once one of these is on them, they’re going to know the seriousness of what they’ve done. They’ve ruined people’s lives.”

VIZ: TANZANIA AFFIDAVIT

VO:
Africrypt was placed in provisional liquidation on April 26, after an investor group launched a liquidation application. In a responding affidavit, filed in Tanzania on 19 July, 2021, Raees Cajee rubbished claims they had absconded with investor funds, or that billions were lost. He placed the figure lost in the alleged hack closer to R72 million.[DM1]

BRENTON: Main card 2, 13.08, T036: 12’38 – 13’24
“As soon as you hear about a guaranteed return – that is immediately a red flag.”

VO: Brenton Naicker is a Fintech, Blockchain and Digital Asset consultant.

MASA: SECOND CAMERA CARD 13.08 - 00016: 00’03’04: “Taking a look at Africrypt, from your understanding, was this a hack or a scam?”

BRENTON: Main card 2, 13.08, T036: 03’22 – 03’43
“If we dig a bit deeper into the details, it holds the hallmarks of a lot of scams that have been run previously. So I can’t say conclusively, but based on what I’ve seen, unfortunately it does look like quite a common scam that’s carried out in this space.”

VO:
Naicker suggests that the unregulated aspect of cryptocurrencies in South Africa makes it a haven for potential scammers.

BRENTON: Main card 2, 13.08, T036: 07’50 – 08’08
“A very important distinction for people to make – and this is for all crypto scams and investments at large – when you send someone cryptocurrency on the blockchain, there is absolutely no centralized body you can phone to say: “Hey, someone scammed me. Can you return these funds? Can you freeze this account?”

MASA: SECOND CAMERA CARD 00016 - 0’08’06 – 0’08’08 - “So you’re on your own?”

BRENTON: Main card 2, 13.08, T036: 08’10 – 08’30
“You’re completely on your own. The software dictates everything. And the software doesn’t have an office you can call or a customer service department. So it’s very important that if you send crypto, you know exactly who you’re sending it to, and you have some sort of accountability in place with that party.”

PIC: C719 Carte Blanche (email) 10 August 2021 S DOLLIE – please highlight last line in point 6

VO:
Shaheed Dollie and Attorneys, the law firm representing the Cajee brothers, declined a request for an interview.

VIZ: (AFFIDAVIT PART 1, PAGE 11/91 POINT 20)
(AFFIDAVIT: C719 Part 3, Pg 3/27 – highlight AMEER’S NAME)

VO: And in yet another twist, the culpability of Ameer Cajee is now being disputed - because of his age, even though he was listed as COO in official communications with investors, and in official company records.
VIZ: (AFFIDAVIT PART 1, PAGE 24/91 POINT 67)
VIZ: C719 Part 3 – Page 9/27 – highlight point 4

VO: Raees Cajee has further alleged that he and his entire family were forced to flee the country – “after receiving numerous death threats”.

VIZ: JUAN MEYER PIC (AWAITING CARTE BLANCHE ARCHIVE FOOTAGE)
PLEASE ALSO USE FRONT PAGE OF AFFIDAVIT – VIZ: BADASPEX VS AFRICRYPT

VO: Court papers allude to the alleged threats being made by controversial West Rand businessman, Juan Meyer.
Meyer’s company, Badaspex, filed the application for the liquidation of Africrypt.[DM2]

VO: Meanwhile, Peirce is confident that it’s only a matter of time before the Cajee’s are extradited to South Africa to face criminal charges for theft, fraud and money laundering.
SEAN: : MAIN CAMERA CARD 2, 13.08, T057, 04’50 – 05’05: “You can run, but you can’t hide. We’re gonna come and find you. As soon as we get that Interpol Red Notice – we’re coming!”


_____________________________________________________________________________________

PROMO 1: (21 sec)
VO: After months of being on the run, law enforcement agencies are closing in on two Joburg brothers at the helm of one of the world’s largest crypto scandals.
DARREN: Second camera card, 13.08, 0002: 00’04’21 – 0’04’48
“We are confident in the South African judicial system and the law enforcement mechanisms that are available when it comes to extradition and bringing them to account in SA.”

PROMO 2: (21 sec)
MASA:

“How did two brothers - barely out of their teens - manage to allegedly scarper billions worth of digital coins from investors off their little-known cryptocurrency platform?”
LUIS: MAIN CARD 1, 12.08, T015: 13’32 –
“There’s so many people who are upset because they built a relationship with a lot of people. They’re not gonna let this go.”

PROMO 3: (11 sec)
VO: As investigations into a R54 billion c[DM3] rypto heist gets underway, a sordid tale of greed, excess and deception by the two young founders has begun to emerge. Will justice prevail?

Producer: Latashia Naidoo | Presenter: Masa Kekana Script: AFRICRYPT SCRIPT: WIKIMEDIA PICS OF AMEER AND RAEES; PICS OF AFRICRYPT LOGO, PICS OF THE UMHLANGA AND THE BALLITO MAGAZINES VO: It was the quintessential rags to riches South African fairytale - of two child prodigies who started a cryptocurrency business out of a tiny bedroom in Robertsham, south of Johannesburg, back in 2013 - before growing it into one of Africa’s largest and most successful AI trading companies. Or so they claimed. PICS: HEADLINES VO: Fast forward to April 2021, when the fairytale turned into a financial nightmare for investors of the brothers’ cryptocurrency investment scheme, Africrypt. VO: On April 13, founders Ameer and Raees Cajee, announced a hack of their AI-driven trading platform – before fleeing the country – allegedly with billions worth of bitcoin from client wallets in tow, in what’s now been alleged to be an ‘exit scam’. PIC: HEADLINE 1 VO: Some estimates put the loss at a mind-blowing $3.6 billion – or R54 billion at the time of the incident. LINK: Main Camera Card 2 1308 - NINJAV_S002_S001_T072 – 00’31 – 01’02 It has all the makings of a major Hollywood blockbuster: two young men with a penchant for supercars, designer labels and private jets; an international manhunt, and billions in stolen cash. But in the real-life version of the Africrypt crypto heist saga, the criminal masterminds are in fact two brothers from Johannesburg – barely out of their teens – who’ve allegedly managed to swindle billions from investors, all while evading local and international authorities. HEADLINE 15; AFRICRYPT BITCOIN SNAPSHOT, BITCOIN WALLET PICS VO: The Cajee brothers allegedly transferred 69,000 bitcoin during the so-called ‘hack’ – to various dark web tumblers and mixers - to make the funds untraceable. FOOTAGE FROM YOUTUBE VIDEO OF LIFESTYLE (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vW9G9vVCopg&t=4s) VO: But who are the so-called “Crypto Brothers” at the helm of what some are calling one of the biggest crypto scams in history? GRAPHIC: PIC – BROTHERS (INVESTOR PRESENTATION AND PICS IN FOLDER) VO: At 21, Raees Cajee is the CEO and founder of Africrypt. In an investor presentation from 2020, he claims to have started the company when he was just 13. And that he first learned of Bitcoin in 2009, and became an early adopter of the cryptocurrency. VO: Brother Ameer Cajee, 18, is the company’s COO – who claims he was a personal equity trader for two years - before branching out into derivative trading. PIC: CAJEES 2 PIC: ABOUT PICS, 20 MONTH TRADING RESULT GRAPHIC SHOWING TIERS VIZ: INVESTOR VIDEO VO: Since Africrypt’s official launch in 2019, the Cajee brothers received millions of rands in deposits from investors who were promised seductive monthly profits of approximately 10% - offered through three tiers of investment packages: Passive, Passive Aggressive, and Aggressive. PIC: AFRICRYPT IPHONE VIDEO (PLEASE ADD THE WORD ‘HACK’ ACROSS); INVESTOR EMAIL – HIGHLIGHT FIRST PARAGRAPH VO: Then came the bombshell announcement: the Africrypt platform had been hacked – allegedly by an unknown and malicious entity in the Ukraine. Ameer Cajee emailed investors on April 13 to tell them that all their bitcoin holdings had been stolen. The brothers fled to the UK shortly after. PIC: INVESTOR EMAIL – HIGHLIGHT THIRD PARAGRAPH DARREN: Second camera card, 13.08, 0001: 03’28 – 03’42 “The person conveying the message also told clients: ‘Do not contact lawyers, do not contact law enforcement, that would only slow down the recovery process.’ That to us was concerning. VO: Darren Hanekom of Hanekom Attorneys is representing a consortium of disgruntled former Africrypt investors. He suggests that a hack of the platform was highly implausible – given that the Cajee brothers were the only ones in control of the private keys to the blockchain network. DARREN: SECOND CAMERA 13.08, 00’55 – 01’08 “If it was indeed a hack, and if it was a hack of the blockchain, it would be the first hack of the bitcoin network.” MASA: MAIN CAMERA CARD 1 12.08, T004, 15’02 – 15’04: “How much money are we talking here?” DARREN: Second camera card, 13.08, 0003: 02’08 – 03’06: “When it comes to the exact amount in question, we’ve seen presentations of the Cajee’s website which alludes to $500m under management. We’ve also seen client totals up to R300m. But then, at the same time, we’ve also observed that the crypto addresses are within the billions. Right now, the only people who know exactly how much is involved, are the Cajee brothers.” VO: For Durban businessman Luis Farais, the Africrypt alleged scam was the ultimate betrayal. Farais developed a close, personal friendship with the entire Cajee family – before their business relationship turned sour. LUIS: Main camera card 1 12.08, T015: 02’27 – 02’57 “In total, over time, as the relationship built, and there was more trust and surety – and I also built that relationship to safeguard my investment… - and I built it up between me and my children to R7.5 million at the time they said to us the supposed hack had happened.” VO: As an established businessman, Farais knew the risks all too well – bitcoin could offer fast ascends on investments, and equally spectacular plunges. But he was convinced by the Cajee brothers of guaranteed returns – and prompted to keep investing more and more. LUIS: Main camera card 1 12.08, T015: 10’46 – 11’15 “After meeting Raees mainly – and Ameer – but the one I dealt with most was Raees, his intelligence was just next level. Some have made him out to be a prodigy – I wouldn’t say that but he’s a very intelligent youngster. And he’s so knowledgeable in terms of the crypto market, in terms of laws around the world. And just so advanced.” LINK: Main Camera Card 2 13.08 - NINJAV_S002_S001_T081 – 00’04 – 00’31 The investors we’ve spoken to all claimed that the Cajee brothers “walked the walk and talked the talk” when it came to crypto investments. They were also unapologetic about flaunting their extensive wealth, as is evident in this video - shot by the Cajee’s friends - which offers a glimpse into their audacious spending habits, and the lifestyle of two young brothers living large and playing hard. PIC: PAGE 177/203 OF BADASPEX AFFIDAVIT (HIGHLIGHT SECOND AMOUNT ON 4 NOVEMBER, 12 NOVEMBER, BIG AMOUNT ON 26 NOVEMBER, 8 DECEMBER, LEATHER JACKETS ON 20 JANUARY) VO: The brother’s lavish spending habits are further illustrated in court papers. Expenses from the company account include: business class tickets to the Maldives for 5 people for R495 000; and R263000 for watches. VIZ: (CAN WE GET A WORLD MAP GRAPHIC AND HIGHLIGHT THESE CITIES IN RED?) VO: Since leaving South Africa in mid-April, the Cajees have been playing cat and mouse with investors and investigators alike - in places like Dubai, Doha, London, the Maldives, and Tanzania. LINK: MAIN CAMERA CARD 12.08, T035, 00’04 – 00’28 The Cajee brothers led an ostentatious lifestyle, which included multi-million rand cars, business class travel to island paradises, and rentals in some of the country’s most upmarket establishments – including the Zimbali Coastal Estate in Ballito, north of Durban, where they allegedly paid R60 000 per month for a year-long rental in a multi-million rand luxury property. GRAPHIC – WORLD MAP WITH VANUATU HIGHLIGHTED VO: In October 2020, Raees Cajee obtained citizenship in the Pacific Island nation of Vanuatu through the country’s citizenship-by-investment scheme, with his brother following suit in January 2021. PIC: VANUATU PAMPHLET VO: Some experts have warned that the scheme is ripe for exploitation, creating a backdoor for visa-free access to the EU and UK. SEAN: MAIN CAMERA CARD 2, 13.08, TO57: 05:44 – 05’54 – “It’s pretty obvious. Why would you get citizenship in another country without extradition orders, if you weren’t planning an exit strategy – or a so-called hack?” VO: Sean Peirce is a specialist investigator who has been mandated by 35 investors to track down the Cajee brothers. SEAN: MAIN CAMERA CARD 2, 13.08, TO57: 02’07 - “These guys are pretty clever with software and algorithms, but they’re not very clever with the law and how bank accounts work, and how we follow the money. And we’ve been following the money!” MASA: 0’06’21 – 0’06’24: “How confident are you that you will be able to cuff them?” SEAN: MAIN CAMERA CARD 2, 13.08, TO57: 08’05 – 08’21: “These kids – and they’re kids – once one of these is on them, they’re going to know the seriousness of what they’ve done. They’ve ruined people’s lives.” VIZ: TANZANIA AFFIDAVIT VO: Africrypt was placed in provisional liquidation on April 26, after an investor group launched a liquidation application. In a responding affidavit, filed in Tanzania on 19 July, 2021, Raees Cajee rubbished claims they had absconded with investor funds, or that billions were lost. He placed the figure lost in the alleged hack closer to R72 million.[DM1] BRENTON: Main card 2, 13.08, T036: 12’38 – 13’24 “As soon as you hear about a guaranteed return – that is immediately a red flag.” VO: Brenton Naicker is a Fintech, Blockchain and Digital Asset consultant. MASA: SECOND CAMERA CARD 13.08 - 00016: 00’03’04: “Taking a look at Africrypt, from your understanding, was this a hack or a scam?” BRENTON: Main card 2, 13.08, T036: 03’22 – 03’43 “If we dig a bit deeper into the details, it holds the hallmarks of a lot of scams that have been run previously. So I can’t say conclusively, but based on what I’ve seen, unfortunately it does look like quite a common scam that’s carried out in this space.” VO: Naicker suggests that the unregulated aspect of cryptocurrencies in South Africa makes it a haven for potential scammers. BRENTON: Main card 2, 13.08, T036: 07’50 – 08’08 “A very important distinction for people to make – and this is for all crypto scams and investments at large – when you send someone cryptocurrency on the blockchain, there is absolutely no centralized body you can phone to say: “Hey, someone scammed me. Can you return these funds? Can you freeze this account?” MASA: SECOND CAMERA CARD 00016 - 0’08’06 – 0’08’08 - “So you’re on your own?” BRENTON: Main card 2, 13.08, T036: 08’10 – 08’30 “You’re completely on your own. The software dictates everything. And the software doesn’t have an office you can call or a customer service department. So it’s very important that if you send crypto, you know exactly who you’re sending it to, and you have some sort of accountability in place with that party.” PIC: C719 Carte Blanche (email) 10 August 2021 S DOLLIE – please highlight last line in point 6 VO: Shaheed Dollie and Attorneys, the law firm representing the Cajee brothers, declined a request for an interview. VIZ: (AFFIDAVIT PART 1, PAGE 11/91 POINT 20) (AFFIDAVIT: C719 Part 3, Pg 3/27 – highlight AMEER’S NAME) VO: And in yet another twist, the culpability of Ameer Cajee is now being disputed - because of his age, even though he was listed as COO in official communications with investors, and in official company records. VIZ: (AFFIDAVIT PART 1, PAGE 24/91 POINT 67) VIZ: C719 Part 3 – Page 9/27 – highlight point 4 VO: Raees Cajee has further alleged that he and his entire family were forced to flee the country – “after receiving numerous death threats”. Meyer’s company, Badaspex, filed the application for the liquidation of Africrypt.[DM2] VO: Meanwhile, Peirce is confident that it’s only a matter of time before the Cajee’s are extradited to South Africa to face criminal charges for theft, fraud and money laundering. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We investigate how two brothers - barely out of their teens - managed to disappear with billions in investors' monies, in one of the world's largest crypto scams
metadata.Unique Selling Point: An international manhunt is underway for two Durban brothers - Ameer and Raees Cajee, the founders of crypto investment firm, Africrypt, who are alleged to have fled the country with an estimated R54 billion worth of crypto assets - all from investors. Thanks to digital forensic evidence and exclusive access to the brothers' bank statements, we go in search of the missing billions, and expose a life of decadence and excess - amassed through lies, fraudulent activities, and selling investors a 'dream'.
metadata.Summary: How did two Durban brothers - barely out of their teens - manage to scarper as much as an alleged R51.27 billion worth of digital coins from investors off their little-known cryptocurrency platform? That’s the question everyone’s been asking since AfriCrypt founders, Raees (21) and Ameer (18) Cajee, first announced a platform “breach” to their investors in April 2021. They claimed that the company had been hacked, and all its cryptocurrency holdings stolen - to the tune of billions of rand. Since then, the brothers have fled the country - purportedly for fear of their lives - all while a sordid tale of greed, excess and deception has been unfolding back home - in what some experts claim could be one of the biggest crypto scams in history. Africrypt claimed to be a wildly successful cryptocurrency investment platform in which investors would send funds for the Cajee brothers to trade. The platform surged in popularity in 2020 as word spread of the huge gains being made, but in 2021 a familiar pattern began to emerge – there were problems with withdrawals, then communications stalled, and finally the platform collapsed, taking investor funds with it. While it’s now understood a group of about 15 investors who have been pressing for liquidation of AfriCrypt had invested about R100 million in the platform, the total amount invested could run into billions - with some putting the figure at $3.6 billion (R51.27 billion.) If correct, this would far exceed the $588 million netted by Mirror Trading International, rated one of the biggest crypto scams of 2020. And while the Financial Sector Conduct Authority’s (FSCA’s) is investigating Africrypt, a group of some 35 investors have now hired Durban-based PI, Sean Peirce, to track down the brothers, piece together the funds’ disappearance, and bring the pair to book. Now investors say they won’t stop baying for blood, until justice is served.
metadata.Further information: I have access to court records, bank statements, and investors who lost tens of millions with AfriCrypt and are willing to speak on record. The investigators further claim that there are other criminal elements to this case - including money laundering. Peirce adds that the Cajee’s “went wild with other people’s monies”, and has visual and social media documentation of the brother’s fleet of super cars, lavish dwellings, private jets, and eye-wateringly expensive family holidays - just months before the reported “hack”.
